Cochrane synthesis highlights small pooled benefits and increased ARIA, with applicability disputed

The class-level synthesis informs benefit–harm discussions, but cannot substitute for drug-specific evidence.

Key quantitative results: Cognition at 18 months: standardized mean difference −0.11 (95% CI −0.16 to −0.06), 13 trials and 9,895 participants; moderate certainty.

ManagementDisease-modifying treatment

Added September 7, 2026 · DOI:10.1002/14651858.CD016297

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

A subsequent peer-reviewed critique challenges pooling mechanistically different and unsuccessful antibodies with current treatments.

Study design

Seventeen randomized trials, 20,342 participants with MCI or mild AD dementia; searches through August 7, 2025.

Key quantitative results

  • Cognition at 18 months: standardized mean difference −0.11 (95% CI −0.16 to −0.06), 13 trials and 9,895 participants; moderate certainty.
  • ARIA-E: approximately 119 versus 12 per 1,000 treated with antibody versus placebo, across 11 trials and 13,595 participants.

What changed

A new synthesis generated a substantive methodological debate.

Strength of evidence

Systematic synthesis with outcome-specific certainty; class-level applicability is contested.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Discuss absolute clinical effects and harms by treatment.

Field medical relevance

Explain both the pooled findings and their limits.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No payer policy changes are established.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Does this prove every approved antibody is ineffective?
No. Pooling diverse agents can obscure treatment-specific effects.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Short follow-up and inconsistent symptomatic-ARIA reporting.
  • Snyder et al. question agent pooling, population heterogeneity and mechanistic conclusions; their article is a perspective, not a new trial.

Primary source · DOI · Full review · Peer-reviewed methodological critique, July 28

Nonino F, et al. Amyloid-beta-targeting monoclonal antibodies for MCI or mild dementia due to Alzheimer’s disease. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. April 16, 2026;CD016297. doi:10.1002/14651858.CD016297. Context: Snyder et al. doi:10.1002/alz.71696.
